extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory; scholars interested in democratic institutions and American constitutional development
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length analytic treatment of institutional causes that mitigate the tyranny of the majority in the United States, focusing on administrative structure, the legal profession, the judiciary, and the jury system.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABSENCE OF CENTRAL ADMINISTRATION
rubrics_metrics.description: The national majority in the United States lacks a centralized administration; the directing power has not extended its activity beyond a limited number of prominent objects and has not regulated secondary affairs of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the central government does not execute all public business itself, it cannot descend into the details of administration; this limits the instruments of tyranny available to a majority. The text argues that freedom is preserved in part because the majority 'has not increased the prerogatives of the central government' and so cannot uniformly enforce its will across the country. If a directing power had both centralized government and centralized administration, 'freedom would soon be banished.'

rubrics_metrics.name: TOWNSHIPS/MUNICIPAL BODIES AS CONCEALED BREAKWATERS
rubrics_metrics.description: Local magistrates (townships, municipal bodies, counties) execute central decisions and act as checks on popular excitement and oppressive laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the central government issues a decree it must entrust execution to agents over whom it often has no control; these local agents therefore 'check or part the tide of popular excitement.' Even if an oppressive law were passed, liberties may be protected in the way the law is executed because 'the majority cannot descend to the details...of administrative tyranny.' The passage presents local execution as a practical restraint on centralized majoritarian despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE PROFESSION OF THE LAW SERVES TO COUNTERPOISE THE DEMOCRACY
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the legal profession provide the most powerful existing security against the excesses of democracy because their habits, studies, and social position give them conservative and aristocratic tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers derive habits of order, taste for formalities, reverence for regular connexion of ideas, and a special body of knowledge that places them in a privileged social station. These traits make them hostile to revolutionary spirit and the unreflecting passions of the multitude, so they act as a stabilizing, aristocratic element within democratic society. The text notes both natural tendencies (order, formalism, contempt for popular judgement) and accidental/circumstantial causes (their role in government, coalescence with aristocracy) that can check or enhance this effect. It also observes limits: lawyers are governed by private interests and may not always oppose innovation; when excluded from political rank they may instead lead revolutionary efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: RELIANCE ON PRECEDENT / COMMON LAW FOSTERS CONSERVATISM
rubrics_metrics.description: The English and American reliance on precedent and the common law produces a legal culture that favors reverence for what is old, timid habits, and slow adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because English and American lawyers 'found their opinions and the decisions of their courts upon the opinions and decisions of their forefathers,' they tend to abnegate original opinion, quote authorities, and prefer regularity and legality over novelty. This creates demand for legal assistance, separates lawyers from the general populace, and helps to maintain legal stability. The passage contrasts this with code-based systems (e.g., France), where statutes are readable by many and the advocate reasons from what should have been done rather than from precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: JUDICIAL POWER AND INDEPENDENCE AS A CHECK
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary, and particularly judges' power to declare laws unconstitutional, is a central means by which the legal profession and the courts check democratic majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The American magistrate 'armed with the power of declaring the laws to be unconstitutional' can interfere in political affairs by preventing the people from acting inconsistently with its own principles. The text warns that innovations that weaken judicial independence—such as frequent re-elections of judges or legislative removal on demand—are dangerous and 'will sooner or later be attended with fatal consequences' for the republican system. Thus judicial independence is presented as an institutional criterion that mitigates majority tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCCUPATION OF PUBLIC STATIONS BY LAWYERS LIMITS DEMOCRATIC EXCESSES
rubrics_metrics.description: Because lawyers are the only enlightened class the people generally trust, they are naturally called to occupy legislative and administrative offices, where they influence law formation and execution and tend to resist radical civil-law innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers fill legislatures and administrations and thereby moderate public policy: the Americans have made many political innovations but few civil-law changes because the majority defers to the legal profession in civil matters and lawyers are disinclined to innovate. The profession's penetration into public life spreads legal habits and language through society, making legal spirit widespread and tempering democratic impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIAL BY JURY CONSIDERED AS A POLITICAL INSTITUTION
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial by jury functions not only judicially but politically: it educates the people, establishes the authority of magistrates, and spreads knowledge of law among the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter introduces trial by jury as an instrument of the sovereignty of the people that deserves comparison with other laws establishing that sovereignty. While its utility for ensuring the best administration of justice (especially in civil cases) may be contested, the political effects are emphasized: it tends to educate citizens, extend the authority of magistrates, and make legal ideas more familiar across society. The passage signals a distinction between jury's judicial merits and its broader civic/political role.

rubrics_metrics.name: HISTORICAL/INSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT MATTERS: DANGER FROM PREVIOUS CENTRALIZATION
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic republic founded in a country with a prior history of centralized administration would risk a far more insufferable despotism than existing absolute monarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that if democratic institutions were transplanted to a people habituated to centralized administration and a single individual's authority, the entrenched administrative apparatus and habits would enable a new majority to exercise more pervasive tyranny. The passage therefore presents the prior administrative character of a society as an important institutional criterion affecting whether democracy will devolve into despotism.
